screens.title: YUM vs DNF — what changed and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: YUM and DNF both manage RPM packages and repositories, but DNF is the modern implementation designed to be faster and more robust. DNF improves dependency resolution and provides a cleaner A P I for programmatic interaction while keeping command syntax familiar for administrators. Practically, RHEL 8 and Fedora use DNF as the default, while older CentOS 7 still relies on YUM. The core claim to remember is that both tools operate on the same RPM package format and the same repository metadata, so many skills transfer directly. For example, updating package metadata uses the same idea: refresh cached metadata and then check updates. A common misconception is that DNF uses a different package format — it does not; it works with RPM files like YUM did. Another misconception is that DNF is entirely incompatible with old scripts; usually existing workflows continue to work because DNF preserves much of the command syntax. A useful practical check is to run a repolist and then perform a small install or upgrade in a test VM to confirm that DNF's resolver behaves as expected. How would you verify a new package behaves correctly after switching to DNF?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › YUM vs DNF
Definition

YUM and DNF, same goal, different implementation

Both tools manage RPM packages via repositories. DNF is the newer tool with improved dependency resolution, a stable API, and better performance on large repositories.

Concrete example
On RHEL 8, dnf upgrade updates installed packages. On CentOS 7, yum upgrade serves the same role but uses the older implementation.
Common misconception
DNF uses a different package format — false. Both operate on RPM files and repository metadata.
Check your understanding
If you inherit a CentOS 7 server, which tool will you expect to use by default, and why might you prefer DNF on newer systems?
Comparison snapshot
YUM
Legacy on older systems; familiar commands, older resolver logic.
DNF
Modern resolver, better performance, and maintained API for tooling.
Key Takeaway

Use the tool appropriate to your distribution: DNF on RHEL 8+ and Fedora, YUM on older systems. The underlying package format remains RPM, so concepts transfer.

screens.title: Refreshing metadata and checking for updates
screens.narratorSegment: Keeping package metadata up-to-date is the first step before installing or upgrading software. The local metadata cache lets DNF know which package versions are available; if it is stale you may not see recent packages. Use the check-update step to view available updates, and use makecache to explicitly refresh the metadata. On many systems DNF refreshes automatically, but in constrained or offline environments an explicit makecache improves predictability. When you are ready to upgrade packages, run the aggregator upgrade command to fetch and install the latest versions. The command handles dependency changes, adding required packages and removing obsolete ones when appropriate. A common mistake is to assume upgrade always preserves behavior; sometimes upgrades replace packages or remove obsolete components, so review the transaction summary before confirming. As a practical workflow: refresh metadata, run a dry check for updates, then schedule or execute an upgrade during maintenance windows. How would you validate that a critical package version changed after an upgrade? Refreshing metadata and checking for updates means refresh metadata with check-update or makecache, then run upgrade to apply available package updates safely.. In practical terms, how to keep package metadata current and check for available upgrades. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Refreshing metadata
Process

Refresh metadata → Check updates → Upgrade

Follow a three-step routine when preparing updates: ensure the metadata is current, inspect pending updates, and then perform a controlled upgrade. This reduces surprises and gives you a chance to review dependency changes.
Typical commands (visual only)
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf upgrade
Misconception
Assuming automatic refresh is enough in all environments. Explicitly running makecache can prevent discrepancies in testing or staging mirrors.
Check your understanding
Why schedule upgrades during maintenance windows, and what might you inspect in the transaction summary before proceeding?
Example scenario
If a critical web server package is due for an upgrade, refresh metadata, run a check-update to see the new version, and then either upgrade the package alone or upgrade the full system during a maintenance window after reviewing dependencies and potential removals.
Key Takeaway

Refreshing metadata and reviewing the update summary helps avoid unexpected removals or incompatible dependency changes during upgrades.

screens.title: Install, remove, and autoremove — practical commands
screens.narratorSegment: Installing and removing packages is the day-to-day work of a sysadmin. The install command fetches the requested package and any required dependencies, prompts for confirmation, and applies the transaction. For example, installing the httpd web server is done with the install command and will display a list of packages that will be added. To remove a package, use the remove command; it typically removes only the package itself and leaves configuration files intact. If you want to clean up dependencies that were installed automatically and are no longer required, run autoremove. A common error is to expect remove to purge configuration files; dnf remove generally does not. Another important point is to read the transaction summary before confirming an install or remove; DNF will flag any required removals and list new packages. A practical habit is to run dnf info on a package first to confirm version and vendor, then proceed. How will you verify no important services were removed during an autoremove? Install, remove, and autoremove — practical commands means use install and remove for package changes and autoremove to clean orphaned dependencies; always review the transaction summary.. In practical terms, commands and expected behavior when adding or removing packages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Install & Remove
Command examples
sudo dnf install httpd
sudo dnf remove httpd
sudo dnf autoremove
sudo dnf info httpd
The install command lists dependencies and asks for confirmation before proceeding. Remove will uninstall the package but usually keep configuration under /etc. Autoremove detects packages with no remaining reverse dependencies and removes them to reclaim space.
Concrete example
Install httpd, verify its version with the package info or service command, then remove it. If libraries installed only for httpd remain, run autoremove to clean them up. Before running autoremove, inspect the list to ensure it does not remove packages needed by other services.
Misconception
Expecting remove to purge configuration. You must clean /etc manually if required.
Key Takeaway

Use dnf info before changes, confirm the transaction summary, and review packages listed for autoremove to avoid removing shared dependencies.

screens.title: Repository (.repo) files — anatomy and parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Repositories are defined by. repo files typically stored in /etc/yum. repos. d. Each repository entry has a unique ID in square brackets, a human-readable name, and either a mirrorlist or a base URL pointing to package locations. Two flags are particularly important: enabled determines whether the repository is active, and gpgcheck instructs the package manager to verify packages with the repository's GPG key. The gpgkey entry points to the public key file. These fields control both availability and security. A typical. repo section contains mirrorlist or baseurl, name, enabled set to 0 or 1, gpgcheck set to 1 to enable verification, and gpgkey pointing to the trusted key. A common mistake is to add a third-party repository without importing its GPG key, which disables verification and risks installing tampered packages. Always verify and import GPG keys from trusted sources before enabling third-party repos. How would you confirm a newly added repository is active and trusted? In practical terms, understand the structure of a .repo entry and why each field matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repo anatomy
keyIdea.text: A .repo file maps a repository ID to locations, enabled state, and GPG verification settings that control both access and security.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › .repo Files
Anatomy
[baseos]
name=CentOS Stream 8 - BaseOS
mirrorlist=http://mirrorlist.centos.org/?release=8-stream&arch=$basearch&repo=BaseOS&infra=$infra
#baseurl=http://mirror.centos.org/centos/$releasever/BaseOS/$basearch/os/
gpgcheck=1
enabled=1
gpgkey=file:///etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-CentOS-Official
This example shows an ID, a name, a mirrorlist, gpgcheck enabled, and a gpgkey path. Either mirrorlist or baseurl is used to locate packages.
Field meanings
  • id: unique repository identifier used with --enablerepo or --disablerepo.
  • mirrorlist/baseurl: location of package metadata and RPM files.
  • enabled: 1 to enable, 0 to disable by default.
  • gpgcheck/gpgkey: enable and point to the GPG public key for package verification.
Misconception
Assuming enabling a repo is safe without importing its GPG key. Always import and trust keys from verified sources.
Key Takeaway

Inspect .repo files to confirm mirror locations, enabled state, and that gpgcheck is set with a valid gpgkey before trusting a repository.

screens.title: Enable, disable and add repositories safely
screens.narratorSegment: Managing repositories means both editing. repo files and sometimes enabling a repository only for a single command. You can temporarily enable a repository with a flag in the command line so you do not permanently change system configuration. For adding third-party repositories, dnf provides helper utilities when the plugins package is available; using config-manager you can add a repo file by URL which simplifies repository installation. Always import the repository's GPG key before enabling installs from it to maintain package security. A common troubleshooting flow for missing packages is to run dnf repolist to confirm the repo exists and is enabled, then run makecache to refresh metadata. If the repository is disabled in its. repo file, change enabled to 1 or use the temporary enable switch. When adding repos, consider the trustworthiness and maintainability of the source and prefer vendor-supplied packaging where possible. What steps will you take to validate a new repo before installing software from it? Enable, disable and add repositories safely means temporarily enable repositories for one-off installs, and use config-manager to add trusted repos while ensuring the gpg key is imported.. In practical terms, how to temporarily enable a repo or add a third-party repo with config-manager. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Enable & Add Repos
Temporary enable
You can enable a repository only for a single command without changing .repo files. This is useful when a repo is disabled by default but you trust it for one package.
Diagnostic commands
dnf repolist
# temporary enable example: dnf --enablerepo=repo-id install package
sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo
Misconception
Adding a repo without its GPG key is safe — false. Always import and trust the GPG key before installing packages from a new repo.
Practical checklist before installing from a new repo
  • Confirm the repo file lists a baseurl or mirrorlist and is enabled if needed.
  • Import and verify the repository's GPG key via its gpgkey path.
  • Run makecache to refresh metadata before installing.
  • Prefer vendor or well-known community repositories like EPEL for additional packages.
Key Takeaway

Enable repositories only as needed and always verify the GPG key. Use config-manager for a repeatable add-repo workflow.

screens.title: GPG keys and package verification
screens.narratorSegment: GPG verification ensures the authenticity and integrity of packages you install. When gpgcheck is set to one in a. repo file, the package manager verifies the downloaded RPM signatures against the public key referenced by gpgkey. If the key is missing or untrusted, package installs may fail or require manual trust decisions, which can be unsafe. This verification prevents attackers from distributing tampered packages via a compromised mirror. A common mistake is to disable gpgcheck to bypass verification; this exposes the system to integrity risks. For third-party repositories, import their public key file into the system keyring and confirm the source before enabling installs. To verify a key, inspect the key fingerprint and compare it to the vendor-provided fingerprint through an out-of-band channel. In practice, keep gpgcheck enabled for all production servers and only disable it temporarily in tightly controlled test environments while you resolve key issues. What steps will you take to validate a GPG fingerprint before trusting a new repository? GPG keys and package verification means always enable and verify gpg checks; add only trusted keys and avoid disabling gpgcheck on production systems.. In practical terms, why gpgcheck and gpgkey are crucial for secure package installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why it matters

GPG verification ensures packages are signed by a trusted publisher and have not been modified in transit. This is a primary defense against supply-chain tampering via compromised mirrors or rogue repositories.

screens.title: Diagnosing missing packages and disabled repositories
screens.narratorSegment: When dnf reports it cannot find a package, the most likely causes are a mis-typed name, a missing or disabled repository, or stale metadata. Start diagnosis by checking the package name with a search; use the search command to see if the package exists under a different name. Next, list enabled repositories with repolist to ensure the repository that should contain the package is present and enabled. If it is disabled, either enable it temporarily for the install or set enabled to one in its. repo file. If the repository is present but the package still cannot be found, refresh the metadata cache with makecache to ensure you have the latest index. Another technique is dnf provides on a filename to map a file to the package that supplies it. If repository misconfiguration caused the issue, inspect the. repo file for correct mirrorlist or baseurl. This step-by-step approach resolves the vast majority of 'unable to find a match' errors and helps you avoid unnecessary configuration changes. screens.title: Dependency conflicts and using dnf history
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency conflicts occur when two packages require incompatible versions of a library or when two packages provide the same file. DNF's resolver is strong, but some conflicts need manual intervention. When you encounter a conflict, inspect the transaction output: DNF will list the conflicting packages and the packages it will add or remove. If an update introduced instability, dnf history is a powerful tool: it lists past transactions and lets you view details, undo a transaction, or rollback to a prior state when a recent change caused issues. Use dnf history info to inspect a transaction, then dnf history undo or rollback to revert changes when appropriate. A common pitfall is to manually remove packages that appear unrelated — instead use history to understand the chain of events and revert a single transaction where possible. For complex dependency problems, consider enabling debuginfo or checking package provides to understand why a particular version was chosen. What is a safe first action when a recent upgrade caused a service outage? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on the package management tools used on Red Hat derivatives: YUM and its successor DNF. You will learn what these managers do, why DNF replaced YUM in newer releases, and how both interact with RPM packages and repositories to install, update, and remove software. We'll walk through routine operations — refreshing metadata, upgrading all packages, installing and removing software, and cleaning up orphaned dependencies — and show how repository configuration and GPG keys affect package authenticity. You will also learn practical troubleshooting steps for missing packages, disabled repositories, and conflicting dependencies. By the end you will be able to configure a repository file, check repository status, run safe upgrades, and use history and provides commands to investigate problems. A short hands-on scenario will demonstrate installing the EPEL repository, installing nginx, and then removing it and cleaning orphaned packages. Keep safety in mind: always use administrative privileges and import and trust GPG keys only from reliable sources.

This chapter sets four practical objectives that will guide our work. First, you will understand the role and architecture of YUM and DNF on Red Hat derivatives, which means recognizing how each tool interacts with RPM packages and repositories. Second, you will be able to perform common package operations: installing software, updating packages, and removing packages safely using the correct commands and flags. Third, you will configure and manage software repositories by reading and editing. repo files, enabling or disabling repositories, and ensuring GPG keys are configured for verification. Finally, you will troubleshoot package management issues such as missing packages, disabled repositories, conflicting dependencies, and use tools like repolist, history, provides, and makecache to diagnose problems. Each objective is practical: for example, when a package cannot be found you will check repolist and refresh the metadata cache. These skills reduce downtime and help keep systems secure and current.

Now we'll translate objectives into hands-on actions you can perform to demonstrate competence. To show understanding of role and architecture, list the enabled repositories and inspect a. repo file to recognize mirrorlist, baseurl, enabled, and gpgcheck entries. To prove package operation skills, install a simple package and verify it runs, then remove it and confirm files remain or are cleaned. For repository management, add or enable the EPEL repository and confirm it appears in the repolist output, and import the repository's GPG key before installing packages from it. For troubleshooting, reproduce a missing-package error, then run a sequence: check repolist, refresh the metadata cache with makecache, search for the package with dnf search, and use provides to map files back to packages. These concrete milestones help you move from theory to safe administration practices on RHEL-family servers.

YUM and DNF both manage RPM packages and repositories, but DNF is the modern implementation designed to be faster and more robust. DNF improves dependency resolution and provides a cleaner A P I for programmatic interaction while keeping command syntax familiar for administrators. Practically, RHEL 8 and Fedora use DNF as the default, while older CentOS 7 still relies on YUM. The core claim to remember is that both tools operate on the same RPM package format and the same repository metadata, so many skills transfer directly. For example, updating package metadata uses the same idea: refresh cached metadata and then check updates. A common misconception is that DNF uses a different package format — it does not; it works with RPM files like YUM did. Another misconception is that DNF is entirely incompatible with old scripts; usually existing workflows continue to work because DNF preserves much of the command syntax. A useful practical check is to run a repolist and then perform a small install or upgrade in a test VM to confirm that DNF's resolver behaves as expected. How would you verify a new package behaves correctly after switching to DNF?

Keeping package metadata up-to-date is the first step before installing or upgrading software. The local metadata cache lets DNF know which package versions are available; if it is stale you may not see recent packages. Use the check-update step to view available updates, and use makecache to explicitly refresh the metadata. On many systems DNF refreshes automatically, but in constrained or offline environments an explicit makecache improves predictability. When you are ready to upgrade packages, run the aggregator upgrade command to fetch and install the latest versions. The command handles dependency changes, adding required packages and removing obsolete ones when appropriate. A common mistake is to assume upgrade always preserves behavior; sometimes upgrades replace packages or remove obsolete components, so review the transaction summary before confirming. As a practical workflow: refresh metadata, run a dry check for updates, then schedule or execute an upgrade during maintenance windows. How would you validate that a critical package version changed after an upgrade? Refreshing metadata and checking for updates means refresh metadata with check-update or makecache, then run upgrade to apply available package updates safely.. In practical terms, how to keep package metadata current and check for available upgrades. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Installing and removing packages is the day-to-day work of a sysadmin. The install command fetches the requested package and any required dependencies, prompts for confirmation, and applies the transaction. For example, installing the httpd web server is done with the install command and will display a list of packages that will be added. To remove a package, use the remove command; it typically removes only the package itself and leaves configuration files intact. If you want to clean up dependencies that were installed automatically and are no longer required, run autoremove. A common error is to expect remove to purge configuration files; dnf remove generally does not. Another important point is to read the transaction summary before confirming an install or remove; DNF will flag any required removals and list new packages. A practical habit is to run dnf info on a package first to confirm version and vendor, then proceed. How will you verify no important services were removed during an autoremove? Install, remove, and autoremove — practical commands means use install and remove for package changes and autoremove to clean orphaned dependencies; always review the transaction summary.. In practical terms, commands and expected behavior when adding or removing packages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Repositories are defined by. repo files typically stored in /etc/yum. repos. d. Each repository entry has a unique ID in square brackets, a human-readable name, and either a mirrorlist or a base URL pointing to package locations. Two flags are particularly important: enabled determines whether the repository is active, and gpgcheck instructs the package manager to verify packages with the repository's GPG key. The gpgkey entry points to the public key file. These fields control both availability and security. A typical. repo section contains mirrorlist or baseurl, name, enabled set to 0 or 1, gpgcheck set to 1 to enable verification, and gpgkey pointing to the trusted key. A common mistake is to add a third-party repository without importing its GPG key, which disables verification and risks installing tampered packages. Always verify and import GPG keys from trusted sources before enabling third-party repos. How would you confirm a newly added repository is active and trusted? Repository (.repo) files — anatomy and parameters means a .repo file maps a repository id to locations, enabled state, and gpg verification settings that control both access and security.. In practical terms, understand the structure of a .repo entry and why each field matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Managing repositories means both editing. repo files and sometimes enabling a repository only for a single command. You can temporarily enable a repository with a flag in the command line so you do not permanently change system configuration. For adding third-party repositories, dnf provides helper utilities when the plugins package is available; using config-manager you can add a repo file by URL which simplifies repository installation. Always import the repository's GPG key before enabling installs from it to maintain package security. A common troubleshooting flow for missing packages is to run dnf repolist to confirm the repo exists and is enabled, then run makecache to refresh metadata. If the repository is disabled in its. repo file, change enabled to 1 or use the temporary enable switch. When adding repos, consider the trustworthiness and maintainability of the source and prefer vendor-supplied packaging where possible. What steps will you take to validate a new repo before installing software from it? Enable, disable and add repositories safely means temporarily enable repositories for one-off installs, and use config-manager to add trusted repos while ensuring the gpg key is imported.. In practical terms, how to temporarily enable a repo or add a third-party repo with config-manager. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GPG verification ensures the authenticity and integrity of packages you install. When gpgcheck is set to one in a. repo file, the package manager verifies the downloaded RPM signatures against the public key referenced by gpgkey. If the key is missing or untrusted, package installs may fail or require manual trust decisions, which can be unsafe. This verification prevents attackers from distributing tampered packages via a compromised mirror. A common mistake is to disable gpgcheck to bypass verification; this exposes the system to integrity risks. For third-party repositories, import their public key file into the system keyring and confirm the source before enabling installs. To verify a key, inspect the key fingerprint and compare it to the vendor-provided fingerprint through an out-of-band channel. In practice, keep gpgcheck enabled for all production servers and only disable it temporarily in tightly controlled test environments while you resolve key issues. What steps will you take to validate a GPG fingerprint before trusting a new repository? GPG keys and package verification means always enable and verify gpg checks; add only trusted keys and avoid disabling gpgcheck on production systems.. In practical terms, why gpgcheck and gpgkey are crucial for secure package installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When dnf reports it cannot find a package, the most likely causes are a mis-typed name, a missing or disabled repository, or stale metadata. Start diagnosis by checking the package name with a search; use the search command to see if the package exists under a different name. Next, list enabled repositories with repolist to ensure the repository that should contain the package is present and enabled.
